evidence: Plaut. Amph. 1062: ut subitō, ut properē, ut validē tonuit!
Ter. Ph. 180: ita nunc imparātum subitō tanta tē impendent mala
terms.comment: The everyday word, in comedy and in prose (Lewis & Short: frequent and classical).

evidence: Liv. 7.26.3: corvus repente in galeā cōnsēdit
Caes. BG 1.52.3: hostēs repente celeriterque prōcurrērunt
Caes. BG 2.3.1: eō cum dē imprōvīsō celeriusque omnium opīniōne vēnisset
Plaut. Rud. 1192: quī ex imprōvīsō fīliam invēnī meam?
terms.comment: What no one saw coming, rather than what happens in a flash.

phrases.latin: subitō nōbīs hodiē Alexandrīnae nāvēs appāruērunt
phrases.english: suddenly today the ships from Alexandria came into view

phrases.latin: ut subitō, ut properē, ut validē tonuit!
phrases.english: how suddenly, how fast, how loud it thundered!

phrases.latin: namque cōnserentī jam manum Rōmānō corvus repente in galeā cōnsēdit, in hostem versus
phrases.english: for just as the Roman closed with him, a raven suddenly landed on his helmet, facing the enemy

repente.against: Lewis & Short rĕpentē, against its own dērepentĕ
repente.html: Verg. A. 2.380, trepidusque repente refugit: the fifth foot, -pente re-, is a dactyl; so Verg. A. 2.465 and 7.27, Lucr. 6.667, Ov. Met. 4.402, Juv. 2.83. The ablative of repēns, with the short -e of the third declension; de Vaan 520, s.v. repēns, prints repente.

sources: Lewis & Short: subeo (subitō) · Lewis & Short: repens (repente) · Lewis & Short: derepente · Lewis & Short: improvisus
